content:
Facts: An heir sought identification and delivery of furniture allegedly bequeathed to him by his mother’s holographic will, claiming the assets were stored in the deceased brother’s home.
Legal framework:
Articles 1362 and 587 ICC; principles on interpretation of wills; burden of proof; Article 96 CPC.
Issue:
Whether a generic testamentary clause concerning household goods allows judicial identification and attribution of specific assets through extrinsic evidence.
Principles applied:
Testamentary interpretation requires a comprehensive assessment of the testator’s intent, including contextual and extrinsic elements, but may not integrate or supplement a will with unexpressed content. A generic disposition lacking specification of the assets bequeathed cannot be judicially completed in the absence of an inventory or precise identifying elements. Photographic and testimonial evidence insufficient to individualize the goods does not satisfy the burden of proof. The judge’s interpretative power does not extend to reconstructing an indeterminate testamentary will. Absent proof of bad faith or gross negligence, rejection of the claim does not justify liability for vexatious litigation under Article 96 CPC.
